data.title: A writer of brighter places.
data.intro: Elise Rowan writes warm, thoughtful fiction about ordinary people, particular places and second chances.

children.text: I am a novelist and short-story writer. I write about ordinary people in specific places, and about the small acts of care that hold a life together. My books are quiet, warm and, I hope, hard to put down.

I grew up in a harbour town where the ferry timetable was more of a suggestion, and I have been trying to write that sense of place ever since. I began as a journalist, spent a decade writing other people's stories, and published my first novel late, which I now think was the best thing that could have happened to it.
How I work

I write by hand in the mornings and type in the afternoons. I read my chapters aloud, to an empty room, until they sound like someone talking. Everything I write goes through at least eight drafts, and most of the good sentences arrive in the sixth.
What I care about

I believe stories can make the world slightly kinder, not by preaching, but by letting us spend time inside someone else's life. I visit libraries, schools and reading groups when I can, and I answer every reader's letter myself.
Writing to me
If you have read one of my books, I would love to hear from you. If you run a reading group or an event, tell me about it on the contact page.

data.title: A guide for reading groups
data.intro: Conversation starters for The Farther Shore, and how to invite the author to your group.

children.text: Questions for conversation
These questions are written for reading groups, but they work just as well for a long walk with a friend.
Nell leaves home to avoid a conversation and ends up in the middle of many. Which of the town's small kindnesses felt most true to you?
The book treats the past as something patient rather than something threatening. Did that change how you thought about your own family stories?
The third step is the only one that tells the truth. What is the truth-telling step in your own home?
If you would like me to join
I visit reading groups in person when I can and online when I cannot. Write to me through the contact page, choose 'Book clubs' as the topic and tell me when you meet. I read every message myself.

data.title: The Farther Shore
data.tagline: A story about what we leave behind — and what still finds us.
data.summary: When a lone writer returns to a windswept coastal town, she discovers that the past isn't gone — it's just waiting for a kinder ending.
data.pull_quote: Mind the third step. It's the only one that tells the truth.
data.where_to_buy:
Your local independent bookshop: ask for it by title
Your public library: request it through your branch
Signed copies for events and book clubs: write to the author's office
Ebook and audiobook editions: formats announced with the publisher

children.text: The ferry did not so much arrive as agree to be there. Nell stood on the wet slats of the quay with her bag between her feet and watched the boatman wind a rope round a post that had been wound round, by the look of it, for a hundred years.
"You're Ines's niece," he said, not asking.
"I didn't know she had one," said Nell. "A niece. I mean, I didn't know I was one."

He looked at her for a moment with the plain interest of a man reading a tide table. "She knew," he said. "She kept your photograph on the dresser. The one from the newspaper, when you were given that prize. Cut it out with the kitchen scissors, so the edge is crooked."

Nell opened her mouth and found nothing in it. Above them the headland rose out of the mist, and on it, small and square and lit in one upstairs window, stood a house that had apparently been waiting for her all along.
"Mind the third step," the boatman called after her. "It's the only one that tells the truth."

Nell Harrow has spent twelve years writing other people's stories and none of her own. When a letter from a solicitor she has never met tells her that her late aunt has left her a narrow house on the headland at Pennyhaven, she goes, intending to sign the papers and leave by the evening tide.

The town has other ideas. The ferry runs when it likes, the only café closes at three, and every person Nell meets seems to remember a version of her family that she was never told. A neighbour who still lays a second place at his table. A lighthouse keeper's daughter who has kept a box of letters for forty years. A harbour that fills with fog on the same afternoon each October, whatever the forecast says.

Over one slow autumn, Nell begins to piece together what her aunt left behind and why she chose to leave it to her. What she finds is not a secret to be exposed but a kindness that was waiting to be finished.
What the book is about

The Farther Shore is a novel about homecoming, grief that has gone quiet, and the small, stubborn ways people look after one another. It is warm without being sweet, and it trusts its readers to find the light on their own.
A reading group guide, with questions about memory, inheritance and second chances, is available on request.

data.title: Lanterns on the Low Water
data.tagline: A river town, a long pole and the people still waiting on the water.
data.summary: A twelve-year-old lamp-lighter learns who is still waiting on the river and who has already come home.

children.text: Every evening at dusk Pia took the long pole from its hooks, climbed the six wet steps to the first lamp and lit it, and every evening the river said something back.

Some nights it was only a murmur. Some nights it was a whole sentence, slow and low, as if the water were trying to remember a name. She never answered. She had been told that you do not answer a river. You simply keep the lamp burning and let it know you are there.

In a river town where the lamps are lit by hand each evening, twelve-year-old Pia Marlow is given the job of keeping them burning through the flood season. The work is meant to be a summer's chore. It becomes the way she learns who is still waiting on the water, and who has already come home.
Lanterns on the Low Water is a quiet novel about duty, weather and neighbours, told in short, bright chapters. It was written for readers of all ages and is a good book to share aloud.

children.text: It rained all morning on the day Mr Adeyemi lent his ladder to the family at number nine, and by evening it had stopped, and the whole street smelled of cut grass and wet brick, and no one could say afterwards how it happened that they were all in the road at once.

Small Weather gathers eleven short stories about ordinary days that turn out to matter: a lost glove, a late train, a neighbour's borrowed ladder, a phone call that arrives a year too late and is still, somehow, on time.

Each story takes place within a single day and a few streets, and each ends on a note of unexpected kindness. They are stories to read one at a time, on the bus, at lunch, or in the quiet before sleep.

data.title: Where The Farther Shore began
data.summary: A fogbound week on the coast, a borrowed notebook and the sentence that started the novel.

children.text: The Farther Shore began with a single sentence I did not write. I read it, on a postcard pinned to the wall of a guesthouse on the north coast, in handwriting I will never be able to trace: "Nothing here is lost, only waiting."

I had gone there to finish something else. The week was fogbound, the ferry stopped twice, and each afternoon I walked to the end of the headland and watched the sea take the horizon back. By the fourth day I had stopped trying to work on the old book and had started a new notebook instead.
A town that kept its promises

Pennyhaven is invented, but the way people look after one another there is not. In the week I stayed, a stranger carried my bag up a hill, a café owner stayed open ten minutes for a late walker and a boy returned a glove I had not yet noticed I had lost.
I wanted to write a book that felt like that: a place where kindness is not a plot twist but the weather.
What I hope you find
If you read it, I hope you finish with the feeling of having been somewhere you would like to go back to. That is all I have ever wanted from a book, and it is all I know how to offer.

data.title: On rereading the books that raised us
data.summary: A shelf of old favourites, a long weekend and what changes when you read a book for the fifth time.

children.text: Last month I took a long weekend and reread four books I had loved at sixteen. I expected to find them smaller than I remembered. Some of them were. One of them was much, much larger.

What changed was not the books but the person holding them. At sixteen I read for plot. At forty I read for the small moments between plot: the meal that is described in two lines, the character who holds a door a second too long.
A short list for slow readers

If you want to try it yourself, pick one book you have not opened for ten years and give it a single quiet evening. Do not take notes. Do not decide in advance what you will find. Just see who turns up.

data.title: A notebook, a cup, a slow morning
data.summary: How my working day starts: one notebook, one cup and a rule about not opening the laptop before ten.

children.text: People ask about my routine as if there were a secret in it. There is not. There is a notebook with a soft cover, a fountain pen that I keep forgetting to refill, and a cup that I bought at a market because the glaze looked like rain on a window.

The rule is simple: nothing with a screen before ten. For the first two hours I write by hand, badly, for as long as the tea stays warm. Most of it is thrown away. A little of it, a sentence or two, survives and gets typed up later.
I used to think this was a ritual to make the work feel more serious. I now think it is just a way of making the day gentler to begin, and a gentle beginning, I have found, is most of the battle.

data.title: What I learned from a book club of eleven
data.summary: An evening with a reading group, a very long table and the question I had never been asked.

children.text: In spring I visited a reading group that had met on the first Thursday of every month for nineteen years. There were eleven of them around a long table, with tea, a lemon cake and the kind of easy honesty that takes decades to build.

They asked me questions I had never been asked. Not "where do you get your ideas" but "which character did you least want to leave?" and "what did you cut that you still miss?" I answered both truthfully and walked home lighter.
If you run a reading group
I enjoy visiting groups in person or online when my schedule allows. Write to me through the contact page with the name of your group, how many of you meet, and the book you have chosen.
